question: Look at the rangoli picture (a round flower-like design with a ring in the centre and four red petals around it). Can you see what repeats in it? What happens to the red petals when the rangoli is rotated by 90° around the centre?
answer: The same petal shape repeats around the centre. When the rangoli is turned by 90° about its centre, the red petals come back exactly onto themselves, and so do the other parts.
steps: Look at the red petals around the centre.
Turn the picture by 90° (a quarter turn) about the centre.
Each petal lands exactly on the next petal, so the pattern repeats.
figure: Rangoli: a design with a ring in the centre and four red petals around it, repeating in a definite pattern.
note: The 90° statement is from the chapter text; the book gives no separate printed answer.

question: Look at the pinwheel picture (a blue figure made of many triangles arranged around a hexagon). Which pattern is repeating? Hint: look at the hexagon first. What figure repeats along each side of the hexagon, what is its shape, and how do these shapes move as you go along the boundary of the hexagon?
answer: The same shape made of triangles is stuck to each side of the hexagon, and it repeats in the same way, one after another, as you go around the boundary of the hexagon.
steps: Find the hexagon in the middle.
See what is stuck to each side: the same blue shape made of triangles.
Going around the boundary, the shape repeats in the same turned position each time.
figure: Pinwheel: a blue figure made of many equal triangles arranged around a central hexagon.
note: Open-ended; the book gives no printed answer and does not name the exact shape on each side.

question: Look at the pictures of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram (a temple tower). What are the symmetries that you see in these beautiful structures? Why is the picture of the clouds not symmetrical?
answer: Each of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram has a vertical line down the middle with the left half matching the right half, and many parts repeat in a pattern (towers, windows, tiers). The clouds have no repeating pattern, so they are not symmetrical.
steps: Imagine a vertical line down the middle of each building.
Check that the left side matches the right side.
Clouds have no repeating pattern, so no symmetry.
figure: Photos: Taj Mahal with matching towers on both sides of a central dome and a pool; Gopuram, a tiered tower narrowing upward; clouds with no pattern.
note: Open-ended; vertical mirror symmetry is the expected answer. No printed answer in the book.

question: A blue triangle has a dotted line down its middle. If you fold the triangle along the dotted line, does one half cover the other half completely? Now look at four puzzle pieces joined together with a dotted line through the middle. Are the two sides mirror halves?
answer: For the triangle: yes, one half covers the other exactly, so they are mirror halves. For the puzzle pieces: no, when folded along the line the left half does not exactly fit over the right half.
steps: Fold the triangle along the dotted line: the halves match exactly.
Fold the puzzle pieces along their dotted line: the bumps and holes on the two sides do not match.
Only an exact match gives mirror halves.
figure: Triangle with a vertical dotted line through the apex and the middle of the base. Four joined puzzle pieces with a vertical dotted line through the middle; the pieces have different knobs and sockets on the two sides.
note: Answer is stated in the chapter text.

book_label: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1, first block)
question: Do you see any line of symmetry in the pictures at the start of the chapter (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?
answer: Yes: the flower has 6 lines of symmetry, the rangoli has 4, and the butterfly has 1. The pinwheel and the cloud have no line of symmetry.
steps: Try folding each picture along different lines.
Count the lines where the two halves match exactly: flower 6, rangoli 4, butterfly 1.
The pinwheel looks symmetric but its halves do not match when folded, and the cloud has no pattern.
figure: Chapter opening pictures: six-petal flower, butterfly with wings open, rangoli with four red petals, blue pinwheel, and a cloud.

book_label: Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1, first block)
question: For each of the following figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry if it exists. The five figures, in order, are: (1) an irregular pentagon-like shape with a notch (arrow-head like), (2) a kite, (3) a quadrilateral with two right angles and a slanted top, (4) an L-shape, (5) a scalene triangle.

parts.question: Arrow-head like pentagon with a notch
parts.answer: 1 line of symmetry (slanted, through its tip and notch)

parts.question: Kite
Quadrilateral with slanted top and two right angles
L-shape
parts.answer: 1 line of symmetry (diagonal through the corner of the L)

parts.question: Scalene triangle

answer: Shape 1 has one line of symmetry (a slanted line through its tip). Shape 2 (kite) has one vertical line of symmetry. Shape 3 has none. Shape 4 (L-shape) has one diagonal line of symmetry through its corner. Shape 5 (scalene triangle) has none.
steps: Fold each shape in your mind and look for a line that makes both halves match.
The kite folds along its vertical diagonal; the L-shape folds along the diagonal through its corner.
The slanted quadrilateral and the scalene triangle have no matching fold.
figure: Five outline shapes in a row: concave arrow-head pentagon, kite, quadrilateral with a right-angled lower left and slanted top, L-shape with equal arms, scalene triangle.
note: The official solution draws only three figures with lines (shape 1, kite, L-shape); the other two are left without lines, which means none. Shape numbering follows the order shown in the book.

book_label: Figures with more than one line of symmetry
question: Does a square have only one line of symmetry? Take a square piece of paper and, by folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
answer: No. A square has 4 lines of symmetry: a vertical fold, a horizontal fold, and the two diagonals.
steps: Fold the square in half vertically, then horizontally.
Fold it along one diagonal, then along the other diagonal.
Each fold makes the two halves overlap exactly, so there are 4 lines.
figure: A square sheet folded four ways: Fold 1 vertical, Fold 2 horizontal, Fold 3 and Fold 4 along the two diagonals; the opened paper shows four crease lines meeting at the centre.
note: Answer (4) confirmed by the solutions for the next question.

question: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?
answer: No, there is no other way to fold the square. A square has 4 lines of symmetry.
steps: The four folds are the vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals.
No other fold line makes the halves overlap.
So the count is 4.

book_label: Figures with multiple lines of symmetry
question: Find all the lines of symmetry of each of three figures: (1) a red outline ring with spiky triangular points around it (like a Koch snowflake), (2) a yellow flower of six curved petals meeting at a red-marked centre, (3) a green looped design with four round loops at the corners and a small square in the centre.
answer: Figure 1: 6 lines. Figure 2: no line of symmetry (it only has rotational symmetry). Figure 3: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals).
steps: Fold each figure in your mind along vertical, horizontal and slanted lines.
Count the lines where both halves match.
The twisted petal flower never matches its mirror image, so no line.
figure: Three figures in a row: red jagged ring-shaped outline with spikes (6-fold, snowflake-like); yellow six-petal flower with overlapping petals twisted like a pinwheel; green four-looped knot design with a square in the middle.
note: Not answered in the book solutions; counts are my own. Figure 1 is a snowflake-like outline, taken as 6 lines (the book later says the Koch snowflake sequence has 6 lines after the first stage); figure 2 taken as 0 lines because the petals overlap in a twisted way. Please verify against the printed picture.

question: We saw that the diagonal of a square is also a line of symmetry. Take a rectangle that is not a square. Is its diagonal a line of symmetry? First see the rectangle and answer, then take a rectangular piece of paper and check by folding along its diagonal whether the two parts overlap.
answer: No. The diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square is not a line of symmetry: when folded along the diagonal the two parts do not overlap.
steps: Cut a rectangle that is longer than it is wide.
Fold along a diagonal.
The corners and sides do not meet, so the halves do not overlap.
figure: A rectangle (longer than it is tall) with a dotted line along its horizontal middle shown for reference.

question: A square has corners labelled A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). When the square is reflected along the vertical line of symmetry, where do A, B, C and D go?
answer: B and C go to the positions earlier held by A and D, and A and D go to the positions earlier held by B and C: A takes the place of B, B the place of A, D the place of C and C the place of D.
steps: Draw the vertical line through the middle.
Each corner moves to the matching corner on the other side of the line, at the same height.
figure: Square ABCD with A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left, and a vertical line through its middle.
note: The text states the result (A takes B's place, D takes C's place).

question: For the same square ABCD (A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left): what if we reflect along the diagonal from A to C? Where do points A, B, C and D go? What if we reflect along the horizontal line of symmetry?
answer: Along diagonal AC: A and C stay where they are, and B and D swap places (D takes B's earlier position and B takes D's). Along the horizontal line: A and D swap places, and B and C swap places (D and C take the places of A and B, and A and B take the places of D and C).
steps: Points on the line of symmetry stay where they are.
A point off the line goes to the matching point on the other side, at the same distance from the line.
For the diagonal AC, B and D are on opposite sides, so they swap.
For the horizontal line, the top corners swap with the bottom corners.
figure: Square ABCD with a vertical line shown in the book figure; the question asks about the diagonal AC and the horizontal middle line.

question: Take a piece of paper and fold it in half. Open it and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half. Press the halves together and open the paper again. What do you see? Is the resulting figure symmetric? If yes, where is the line of symmetry? Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts? Try making more such patterns.
answer: You see a blot pattern with the same shape on both sides of the crease. Yes, it is symmetric and the fold (crease) is the line of symmetry. Usually no other line works, since the shape is random, so there is just one line of symmetry.
steps: Fold the paper in half and put ink on one half.
Press the halves together and open: the ink prints a mirror image on the other half.
The crease is the line of symmetry.
note: Open-ended activity; 'usually no other line' is the expected answer for a random blot.

question: In two pictures, a sheet of paper is folded and a cut is made along the dotted line shown (the dotted line forms a notch shape starting at the fold). Draw a sketch of how the paper will look when unfolded. Do you see a line of symmetry in this figure? What is it?
answer: The unfolded paper has a hole (or cut-out) whose shape is the cut shape and its mirror image joined together along the fold. Yes, the fold line is the line of symmetry.
steps: Imagine opening the folded sheet.
The cut shape appears on both sides of the crease, as mirror images.
The crease is the line of symmetry.
figure: Green folded sheet with a dotted cut-line, and a hand cutting along it with scissors.

question: Make different symmetric shapes by folding and cutting. Use thin rectangular coloured paper, fold it several times and cut out intricate patterns, like the blue star-shaped cut-outs shown. Identify the lines of symmetry in the repeating design.
answer: Any such cut-out is symmetric about each of its fold lines. For example, the eight-pointed star shown has 8 lines of symmetry.
steps: Fold the paper several times.
Cut some shapes along the edges and corners.
Open it: every crease is a line of symmetry of the repeating design.
figure: A row of small blue diamonds and three blue eight-pointed star shapes made by folded paper cutting.
note: Open-ended; the 8 lines for the shown star is my reading of the picture.

book_label: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: In each of the following figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet of paper and then the paper was unfolded. Identify the line along which the paper was folded. The four unfolded sheets show: (a) two holes in the left and right sides at the same height; (b) two holes close together near the top right corner; (c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other; (d) four holes, one near each corner. Figure (d) was created by punching a single hole. How was the paper folded?

parts.label: a
parts.question: two holes, one on the left and one on the right at the same height

parts.label: b
parts.question: two holes close together near the top right corner
parts.answer: fold along the diagonal from bottom left to top right

parts.label: c
parts.question: two holes on the right edge, one above the other

parts.label: d
parts.question: four holes near the four corners (made with a single hole)
parts.answer: fold vertically and then horizontally (or vice versa), then punch one hole

answer: (a) a vertical fold through the middle; (b) a diagonal fold (from bottom left to top right) between the two holes; (c) a horizontal fold through the middle between the two holes; (d) the paper was folded vertically and then horizontally (or the other way round), and one hole was punched through all four layers.
steps: The fold line is the line of symmetry, halfway between each pair of matching holes and at right angles to the line joining them.
For (d), four holes means two lines of symmetry: fold in half, then in half again.
figure: Four squares: a) two holes at left and right middle; b) two holes near top right corner; c) two holes on the right edge upper and lower; d) four holes near the four corners.

book_label: Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Given the line(s) of symmetry, find the other hole(s). Five shapes each show one hole and a dashed line of symmetry: (a) a square with a diagonal from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left; (b) a square with a horizontal middle line and a hole in the lower right; (c) an equilateral triangle with a vertical line through the apex and a hole just left of the line near the middle; (d) a circle with a slanted diameter and a hole above the line near the right; (e) a circle with a diagonal line from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left, close to the line.

parts.label: a
parts.question: square, diagonal line, hole near top left
parts.answer: mirror hole across the diagonal, near the top edge

parts.label: b
parts.question: square, horizontal middle line, hole lower right
parts.answer: mirror hole in the upper right directly above

parts.label: c
parts.question: triangle, vertical line, hole left of the line
parts.answer: mirror hole to the right of the line at the same height

parts.label: d
parts.question: circle, slanted diameter, hole above the line

parts.label: e
parts.question: circle, diagonal line, hole near top left
parts.answer: mirror hole on the other side of the diagonal

answer: In every shape the other hole is the mirror image of the given hole in the dashed line: same distance from the line, on the opposite side. (a) the other hole is across the diagonal, near the top edge; (b) in the upper right, directly above the given hole; (c) to the right of the vertical line at the same height; (d) below the slanted line, mirrored; (e) on the other side of the diagonal, mirrored.
steps: Draw a line from the given hole that meets the dashed line at a right angle.
Go the same distance past the dashed line.
Mark the new hole there.
figure: Five shapes with a dashed line of symmetry and one hole each: square with diagonal, square with horizontal line, triangle with vertical line, circle with slanted diameter, circle with diagonal line.
note: Positions of the other holes follow the solution pictures; exact placement is by reflection.

book_label: Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Here are some questions on paper cutting. Consider a vertical fold. We represent it by a picture of a sheet folded in half vertically with an arrow. Similarly, a horizontal fold is represented by a sheet folded in half horizontally with an arrow.
answer: This is an introduction with no question to answer: a vertical fold folds the sheet along a vertical line, and a horizontal fold folds it along a horizontal line. These are used in the next question.
steps: A vertical fold makes a vertical crease.
A horizontal fold makes a horizontal crease.
figure: Two small pictures: a sheet folded vertically (with an arrow) and a sheet folded horizontally (with an arrow).
note: Q3 only sets up notation for Q4 and has no question or answer; included for completeness.

book_label: Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: After each of the following cuts, predict the shape of the hole when the paper is opened. After you have made your prediction, make the cutouts and verify your answer. (a) A green sheet is folded once; a wavy cut is made from the edge, along a dotted line, with a narrow pinched middle. (b) A green sheet is folded once; a cut shaped like a notched banner (with an arrow-head notch) is made. (c) A purple sheet is folded vertically and then horizontally (4 layers) and notches are cut at the corner and edge. (d) A yellow sheet is folded vertically once and rectangular notches are cut along the open edge.

parts.label: a
parts.question: green sheet folded once, wavy cut near the open edge
parts.answer: bow-tie shaped hole with wavy sides, symmetric about the fold line

parts.label: b
parts.question: green sheet folded once, banner-shaped cut with an arrow-head notch
parts.answer: banner shaped hole with notched ends, symmetric about the fold line

parts.label: c
parts.question: purple sheet folded twice (vertical then horizontal), notches cut
parts.answer: opened sheet has edge and corner notches and small rectangular holes arranged symmetrically about both fold lines

parts.label: d
parts.question: yellow sheet folded vertically, notches cut along the open edge
parts.answer: rectangle with a square hole in the middle and notches on both side edges

answer: In every case the opened paper shows the cut shape together with its mirror image in each fold line. (a) a bow-tie like shape with wavy sides, symmetric about the fold line; (b) a banner shape with an arrow-head notch at each end, symmetric about the fold line; (c) a sheet with notches at the edges/corners and small rectangular holes arranged symmetrically on both sides of the vertical and the horizontal fold; (d) a rectangle with notches on both the left and right edges and a square hole in the middle.
steps: Picture opening the sheet.
The cut appears again on the other side of each fold, as a mirror image.
With two folds, the cut appears four times (once in each quarter).
figure: Four folded-paper cutting pictures: (a) green folded sheet with wavy dotted cut; (b) green sheet with banner-like notch cut; (c) purple sheet folded twice with corner notches cut; (d) yellow sheet folded once with notches cut on the open edge. Solutions show the opened sheets.
note: Predicting is open ended; answers describe the solution pictures. Details of (c) and (d) are described approximately from the solution images.

book_label: Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Suppose you have to get each of these shapes with some folds and a single straight cut. How will you do it? (a) The hole in the centre is a square (sides parallel to the sides of the sheet). (b) The hole in the centre is a square (tilted so that its corners point up, down, left and right). Note: for the above two questions, check if the 4-sided figures in the centre satisfy both the properties of a square.

parts.label: a
parts.question: square hole in the centre with sides parallel to the paper
parts.answer: fold horizontally then vertically, then cut a small square at the closed corner

parts.label: b
parts.question: tilted square hole in the centre
parts.answer: fold horizontally then vertically, then cut along a slanting line at the closed corner

answer: (a) Fold the paper horizontally and then vertically. At the closed corner (the corner that is the centre of the sheet) cut a small square with all sides closed, using straight cuts parallel to the folds. (b) Fold the paper horizontally and then vertically. At the closed corner cut along one slanting (diagonal) line so that a small triangle is removed; opening gives a tilted square.
steps: Fold twice so that the centre of the sheet is at one corner of the small folded square.
For (a) cut off a small square at that corner.
For (b) cut a slanting line across that corner, removing a triangle.
Open the sheet: the four mirror copies join to make the hole.
figure: Two pink squares, each with a single square hole in the centre: (a) sides parallel to the paper; (b) tilted by 45°.
note: In the book, both parts say 'a square'; part (b) shows the tilted one.

book_label: Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: How many lines of symmetry do these shapes have? (a) a square drawn tilted like a diamond, and an eight-pointed star shape; (b) a triangle with equal sides and equal angles; (c) a hexagon with equal sides and equal angles.

parts.label: a
parts.question: square drawn like a diamond; eight-pointed star

parts.label: b
parts.question: triangle with equal sides and equal angles

parts.label: c
parts.question: hexagon with equal sides and equal angles

answer: (a) tilted square: 4; eight-pointed star: 8. (b) equilateral triangle: 3. (c) regular hexagon: 6.
steps: For a regular shape, the number of lines equals the number of sides.
A square has 4, an equilateral triangle 3 and a regular hexagon 6.
The eight-pointed star has 8 lines through its points and notches.
figure: (a) a tilted square and an eight-pointed star shape; (b) an equilateral triangle; (c) a regular hexagon.

book_label: Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Trace each figure and draw the lines of symmetry, if any. There are eight figures: four rhombus-pattern figures (1: one rhombus sitting on top of two rhombi that touch each other; 2: three rhombi in a row joined at their left-right corners; 3: a large diamond made of four small rhombi; 4: four rhombi in two columns of two, overlapping, standing in an X-like arrangement) and four figures on squared grids (5: a square inside a bigger square with the inner square divided into four; 6: an octagon-like shape with long vertical sides; 7: a five-sided shape like a kite with a flat right side; 8: a four-pointed star).

parts.question: rhombus pattern 1 (one rhombus above two)
three rhombi in a row
large diamond of four rhombi
four overlapping rhombi, two columns
square inside a square on grid
octagon-like shape on grid
five-sided shape on grid
four-pointed star on grid

answer: 1: 1 line (vertical). 2: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 3: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 4: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical). 5: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals). 6: 2 lines (vertical and horizontal). 7: 1 line (horizontal). 8: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and two diagonals).
steps: Trace the figure on paper or imagine folding it.
Try vertical, horizontal and diagonal folds.
Count the folds where the two halves overlap.
figure: Four figures made of small rhombi, then four red figures on squared grids: nested squares, a long octagon-like shape, a five-sided kite-like shape, a four-pointed star.
note: Counts are read from the solution picture, in the same order the book shows the figures.

book_label: Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Find the lines of symmetry for the kolam below. The kolam is a large six-sided (hexagonal) pattern made of dots and star shapes made of rhombi, with the same design repeating around the centre.
answer: The kolam has 6 lines of symmetry: one vertical line, one horizontal line and four slanted lines, all through the centre.
steps: Look for lines through the centre where one side matches the other.
The pattern repeats 6 times around the centre, so there are 6 lines.
figure: A kolam: a hexagonal arrangement with star-flower motifs made of rhombi and small rhombi between them, with one motif at the centre.
note: PLEASE CHECK: count of 6 is inferred from the solution picture, which shows dashed lines through the centre at equal angles (vertical, horizontal and four slanted); the book text prints no number.

book_label: Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Draw the following. (a) A triangle with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry. (c) A triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?

parts.label: a
parts.question: triangle with exactly one line of symmetry

parts.label: b
parts.question: triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry

parts.label: c
parts.question: triangle with no line of symmetry

parts.label: d
parts.question: Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?

answer: (a) An isosceles triangle (two equal sides, third side different). (b) An equilateral triangle. (c) A scalene triangle (all sides different). No, it is not possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry.
steps: Two equal sides give one line: the line from the apex to the middle of the base.
All three sides equal give three lines.
If a triangle has two lines of symmetry it is forced to have all three, so exactly two cannot happen.

book_label: Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Draw the following. In each case, the figure should contain at least one curved boundary. (a) A figure with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A figure with exactly two lines of symmetry. (c) A figure with exactly four lines of symmetry.

parts.label: a
parts.question: exactly one line of symmetry, with a curved boundary
parts.answer: for example a semicircle, or a symmetric shape with a round head

parts.label: b
parts.question: exactly two lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary
parts.answer: for example an ellipse, or a shape with round bumps on top and bottom

parts.label: c
parts.question: exactly four lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary
parts.answer: for example a square with a round bump on each of its four sides

answer: Any correct drawing works. Example: (a) a semicircle (one line, perpendicular to the straight edge) or a shape with a round top and a symmetrical body; (b) an ellipse or a rectangle with rounded bumps at the top and bottom (vertical and horizontal lines); (c) a circle-bump flower of four equal round loops around a square (4 lines).
steps: Start with a symmetric shape such as a square or an arrow shape.
Replace some edges by curves, placing the same curve on each matching side.
Count the lines to check.
note: Drawing task; any correct drawing is accepted. A circle does not count for (c) as it has infinitely many lines.

book_label: Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Copy the following on squared paper. Complete them so that the blue line is a line of symmetry. Problem (a) has been done for you. (b) A stepped red shape above a horizontal blue line, with a slanted edge ending at the right end of the line. (c) A staircase-shaped red outline next to a slanted (diagonal) blue line. (d) A small red shape touching a vertical blue line on a narrow grid. (e) A red five-sided outline hanging below a horizontal blue line. (f) A red outline with corner cuts next to a diagonal blue line. Hint: for (c) and (f), see if rotating the book helps!

parts.label: b
parts.question: red stepped shape above a horizontal blue line
parts.answer: mirror the shape below the line (the solution shows a matching shape with steps below)

parts.label: c
parts.question: staircase outline beside a diagonal blue line
parts.answer: mirror across the diagonal: the staircase repeats on the other side

parts.label: d
parts.question: small shape on a vertical line
parts.answer: mirror it on the other side of the vertical line

parts.label: e
parts.question: five-sided red outline hanging below a horizontal line
parts.answer: mirror it above the line to complete a symmetric figure

parts.label: f
parts.question: red outline with corner cuts beside a diagonal line

answer: In each case, reflect every point of the red outline in the blue line: draw each mirror point at the same distance on the other side, then join the mirror points. The finished shape is symmetric about the blue line. (b) the shape is mirrored below the horizontal line; (c) mirrored across the diagonal; (d) the left red part is mirrored to the right of the vertical line; (e) mirrored above the horizontal line; (f) mirrored across the diagonal.
steps: Pick a corner of the red outline and count its distance from the blue line.
Go the same distance on the other side and mark the mirror corner.
Join the mirror corners in the same order.
For a diagonal line, turn the page so that the line is vertical or horizontal.
figure: Six grid pictures (a to f), each with a red partial outline and a blue line (vertical, horizontal or diagonal) that is to be a line of symmetry; (a) is already completed.
note: Drawing task; answers describe the solution pictures. Part (a) is already given in the book.

book_label: Figure it Out Q12 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Copy the following drawing on squared paper. Complete each one of them so that the resulting figure has the two blue lines as lines of symmetry. (a) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red horizontal segment near the bottom; (b) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red broken vertical segment with a point on the left; (c) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a stepped red outline in the upper left; (d) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red corner outline in the lower left; (e) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red zigzag in the upper right; (f) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red outline in the lower left.

parts.label: a
parts.question: diagonals, red bottom segment

parts.label: b
parts.question: diagonals, red left zigzag
parts.answer: four-pointed notched figure (a point on each side)

parts.label: c
parts.question: vertical and horizontal, stepped upper-left outline

parts.label: d
parts.question: vertical and horizontal, lower-left corner outline

parts.label: e
parts.question: vertical and horizontal, upper-right zigzag
parts.answer: symmetric stepped cross shape with notched ends

parts.label: f
parts.question: vertical and horizontal, lower-left outline

answer: Reflect the red part in the first blue line, then reflect the whole result in the second blue line. Then the figure is symmetric about both. (a) completes to a square; (b) completes to a four-sided figure with an arrow-head point on each side; (c) a symmetric cross-like stepped shape; (d) a symmetric octagon-like shape; (e) a symmetric stepped cross shape with a notched top and bottom; (f) a symmetric butterfly-like shape.
steps: Reflect the given red part in one blue line.
Reflect the new figure (old plus new) in the other blue line.
Check that both blue lines now act as folds.
figure: Six grid pictures (a to f), each with two blue lines (two diagonals in a and b; a vertical and a horizontal in c to f) and part of a red figure to be completed.
note: Drawing task; descriptions of results are from the solution pictures and approximate.

book_label: Figure it Out Q13 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)
question: Copy the following on a dot grid. For each figure draw two more lines to make a shape that has a line of symmetry. The six dot-grid figures each show a few connected line segments.
answer: Any correct completion works. For each figure choose a mirror line (it can be vertical, horizontal or slanted), then draw the mirror images of the two end points to close the shape with two extra lines. The solutions show closed shapes (four-sided or five-sided) each with one drawn line of symmetry.
steps: Look at the open figure and imagine a line that could be a mirror.
Mark the mirror image of each end of the open figure.
Join these to complete the two lines.
figure: Six dot-grid pictures, each with an open figure made of a few straight segments; two segments must be added in each to make a symmetric shape.
note: Drawing task; there can be more than one correct answer. The book solution shows one choice per figure.

question: A paper windmill with 4 equal blades looks the same when turned by 90° about the red point at its centre. Will the windmill look exactly the same when rotated through an angle of less than 90°?
answer: No
steps: Turn the windmill by a small angle, say 45°.
The blades do not land on the blades again.
The first turn that makes it look the same is 90°, so no smaller angle works.
figure: Paper windmill with four blades in two shades of green and a red dot at the centre.
note: Book answers 'No!' in the text itself; not in the solutions pages.

book_label: In-text question (section 9.2, four angles of symmetry)
question: The windmill has exactly 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. Do you know of any other shape that has exactly four angles of symmetry?
answer: Yes, a square (also a plus sign made of 4 equal arms, or a pinwheel with 4 equal blades).
steps: A shape with 4 angles of symmetry matches itself after each quarter turn.
A square does this: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
A plus sign with 4 equal arms does the same.
note: Book leaves this open and moves straight to the square.

question: How many angles of symmetry does a square have? How much rotation does it require to get the initial square?
answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. The square overlaps itself after a 90° rotation (A goes to B, B to C, C to D, D to A); it is back in its starting position after 360°.
steps: Rotate the square about its centre by a quarter turn: it overlaps itself.
Each further quarter turn does the same: 90°, 180°, 270°.
A full turn of 360° brings every corner back to its own place.
figure: Square ABCD with a dotted reference line from the centre; after rotating 90° the corners A, B, C, D sit where B, C, D, A were, and the dotted line has turned a quarter turn.

question: A square gets back onto itself after a 90° rotation. Do you know where to mark the centre of rotation?
answer: At the centre of the square, the point where its two diagonals cross.
steps: The centre of rotation is the fixed point that does not move.
In a square this is the middle point.
It is where the diagonals meet.

question: What are the other angles of symmetry of a square (besides 90°)?
steps: Rotate the square by 180° (half turn): it overlaps itself.
Rotate by 270° (three-quarter turn): it overlaps itself.
Rotate by 360° (full turn): it is back where it started.
figure: Three pictures of square ABCD turned by 180°, 270° and 360° with the dotted reference line shown after rotation.

question: Find the angles of symmetry of the following strip. The strip is a trapezium shape (the top side is shorter than the bottom side, the two slanting sides are equal) with a dot marking its centre.
answer: Only 360°. The strip does not have rotational symmetry.
steps: Rotate the strip by 180° about its centre: the longer side is now on top.
This does not overlap the original, because the top and bottom sides are different.
Another 180° gives the original, so only the full turn 360° works.
figure: Trapezium with shorter side on top and longer side at the bottom, with a dot at the centre; second picture is the same trapezium upside down.
note: Book's worked example; answer given in the text.

question: After the strip is rotated by 180° about its centre, does it overlap with the original strip? Why?
answer: No. After 180° the shorter side is at the bottom and the longer side at the top, so it does not fit the original.
steps: Look at the top and bottom sides of the strip.
They are different in length.
A half turn swaps them, so the picture changes.

question: A picture has 4 radial arms (a plus-shaped figure with 4 equal arms), and the angle between adjacent central dotted lines is 90°. How many angles of symmetry does it have? What are they?
answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
steps: The arms are equal and 90° apart.
Each quarter turn moves an arm onto the next arm.
So the turns 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° all work.
figure: Plus shape of 4 equal rectangular arms with dotted lines through them meeting at 90° at the centre.

question: Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that the figure still has 4 angles of symmetry? Try drawing it.
answer: Not if the arms are identical and only the angles are changed: the 4 arms must stay equally spaced, with 90° between neighbours. Changing the angles gives fewer angles of symmetry.
steps: For 4 angles of symmetry, a quarter turn must put each arm on the next arm.
So all four angles between neighbouring arms must be equal.
They must add to 360°, so each is 90°.
note: Book gives no answer here; it asks the child to try and check with paper cutouts.

question: To check if a figure with radial arms has 4 angles of symmetry, draw it on two pieces of paper. Cut out the radial arms from one paper, keep the figure on the other paper fixed, and rotate the cutout to check for rotational symmetry.
answer: A correct check shows the cutout fits exactly onto the fixed figure at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° only.
steps: Draw the figure twice and cut out one copy.
Pin the cutout at the centre and turn it over the other copy.
Count the turns after which it fits exactly.
note: Hands-on task; no written solution.

question: How will you modify the plus-shaped figure with 4 radial arms so that it has only two angles of symmetry?
answer: Make opposite arms alike but the two pairs different, for example the book's figure where the top arm bends to the right at its end and the bottom arm bends to the left (a half turn copy), with the left and right arms straight. Then only 180° and 360° work.
steps: Change the figure so a quarter turn no longer fits.
Keep it the same after a half turn (180°).
Then the angles of symmetry are only 180° and 360°.
figure: Plus-shaped figure whose top arm ends with a step going right and bottom arm ends with a step going left, left and right arms straight, dotted lines through the centre.
note: Book's picture ('Here is one way') appears on the next page; no separate solution entry.

question: Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can you use radial arms for this?
answer: Yes: use 3 equal radial arms placed 120° apart.
steps: 3 angles of symmetry means 3 turns that fit, including 360°.
3 equal arms at equal gaps share the full turn equally.
Each gap is 360° ÷ 3 = 120°.

question: A figure has 3 radial arms but the angles between the arms are not equal. How many angles of symmetry does it have and what are they?
answer: Only 360°, so it has no rotational symmetry.
steps: Trace and cut out a copy of the figure.
Turn the cutout over the figure.
It fits only after a full turn of 360°.
figure: Three radial arms (long thin rectangles with dotted centre lines) meeting at a dot, with unequal gaps between them.
note: Answer stated in the text.

question: Can anything in the three-arm figure be changed to make it have 3 angles of symmetry? Can it be done by changing the angles between the dotted lines?
answer: Yes, make all three angles between adjacent dotted lines equal to 120°.
steps: Make the three angles between the arms equal.
They share a full turn of 360°.
Each is 120°.

question: If a figure with three radial arms has rotational symmetry, a rotated copy must overlap the original. What can you tell about the angles ∠A, ∠B and ∠C between the arms? What must this angle be?
steps: ∠A must overlap ∠B, ∠B must overlap ∠C and ∠C must overlap ∠A.
So the three angles are equal.
They share 360°, so each is 360° ÷ 3 = 120°.
figure: Two rough diagrams of the same 3-arm figure, one turned, with the three angles labelled A, B and C.

question: A 3-arm figure has 120° between adjacent arms. How many angles of rotation does it have and what are they?
answer: 3 angles of symmetry: 120°, 240°, 360°.
steps: After 120° each arm lands on the next arm.
After 240° (120° + 120°) it fits again.
After 360° (120° + 120° + 120°) it is back to the start.
figure: Four pictures of the 3-arm figure (arms coloured): initial position, after 120°, after 240° and after 360° rotation.

question: Can you draw a figure with radial arms that has a) exactly 5 angles of symmetry, b) 6 angles of symmetry? Also find the angles of symmetry in each case. Hint: Use 5 radial arms for the first case. What should the angle between two adjacent radial arms be?

parts.label: a
parts.question: Figure with radial arms having exactly 5 angles of symmetry; list the angles.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Figure with radial arms having 6 angles of symmetry; list the angles.

steps: For n equal arms the gap between neighbours is 360° ÷ n.
5 arms: 360° ÷ 5 = 72°. Multiples of 72° up to 360°.
6 arms: 360° ÷ 6 = 60°. Multiples of 60° up to 360°.
figure: Solution shows 5 narrow equal wedge arms evenly spaced around a centre for (a), and a 6-petal flower for (b).
note: Drawing task; the solution pictures show 5 equal arms and 6 equal petals.

question: Consider a figure with radial arms having exactly 7 angles of symmetry. What will be its smallest angle of symmetry? Is the number of degrees a whole number in this case? If not, express it as a mixed fraction.
answer: 360° ÷ 7 = 51 3/7°. It is not a whole number.
steps: 7 equal arms share the full turn of 360°.
360 ÷ 7 = 51 with remainder 3.
So the smallest angle is 51 3/7°, not a whole number.

book_label: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2, first block)
question: Find the angles of symmetry for the given figures about the point marked with a dot. (a) A plus shape made of a vertical rectangle and a horizontal rectangle of the same length crossing at their middles, dot at the centre. (b) A vertical line with a dot at its middle, and a small square on the right of the top end and another small square on the right of the bottom end. (c) A horizontal segment joining the middles of two long vertical lines (a sideways H), dot at the middle of the horizontal segment.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Plus shape of two equal rectangles.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Vertical line with a small square on the right of each end.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Horizontal bar joining two vertical lines.

steps: Rotate each figure about the dot and see after which turns it fits itself.
(a) a quarter turn fits, so 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
(b) a half turn puts the top square on the left side of the bottom, so it does not fit: only 360°. (c) a half turn fits: 180°, 360°.
figure: (a) plus of two equal rectangles with dot at centre; (b) vertical line with small squares at the right of top and bottom ends, dot at middle; (c) two vertical lines joined by a horizontal segment, dot at its middle.

book_label: Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2, first block)
question: Which of the following figures have more than one angle of symmetry? The seven figures are: a circle with a cross dividing it into 4 equal parts; a downward-pointing triangle with a dot inside; a circle divided into 3 equal parts by three spokes; a four-bladed pinwheel with a red cross; an X made of two crossing lines; a five-pointed star with a dot at its centre; a shape like the letter B made of a vertical line with two half circles on its right.
answer: Five figures: the circle with the cross (4 equal parts), the circle with 3 equal parts, the four-bladed pinwheel, the X, and the five-pointed star.
steps: Test each figure by turning it about its centre.
The circle with 4 parts (order 4), circle with 3 parts (order 3), pinwheel (order 4), X (order 4) and star (order 5) all fit again before a full turn.
The triangle (as drawn) and the B-shape only fit after 360°.
figure: Two rows: circle with cross; downward triangle with dot; circle with 3 spokes; four-bladed pinwheel; X; five-pointed star; B-like shape.
note: Solution lists the cross circle, 3-spoke circle, pinwheel, X and star. The triangle is drawn taller than an equilateral one, so it has one angle only.

book_label: Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2, first block)
question: Give the order of rotational symmetry for each figure: (a) a slanted line with a small flag at its top left end and another small flag at its bottom right end, dot at its middle; (b) an X made of two crossing lines with an angle marked at the top; (c) a six-pointed star with a dot at the centre; (d) three bent arms with fists arranged around a centre; (e) a plus shape made of two rectangles with a dot at the centre; (f) a regular pentagon with a dot at the centre.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Slanted line with flags at its two ends

parts.label: b
parts.question: X of two crossing lines

parts.label: c
parts.question: Six-pointed star

parts.label: d
parts.question: Three bent arms with fists

parts.label: e
parts.question: Plus shape

parts.label: f
parts.question: Regular pentagon

steps: Order of rotational symmetry means the number of angles of symmetry, counting 360°.
Count how many times the figure fits itself in one full turn.
(a) 180° and 360°: 2. (c) 6 points: 6. (d) 3 arms: 3. (f) 5 sides: 5.
figure: Six figures in two rows: flagged line, X with an angle arc, six-pointed star, three-armed figure with fists, plus shape, regular pentagon.
note: Order for (b) is 4 as given in the book solutions; this needs the two crossing lines to be equal and at 90°.

question: Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 2 of them: 180°, 360°. Exactly 3 of them: 120°, 240°, 360°. Exactly 4 of them: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. In each case, the angles are the multiples of the smallest angle. Will this always happen? What do you think?
answer: Yes, the angles of symmetry are always multiples of the smallest angle of symmetry.
steps: Turning by the smallest angle twice is the same as turning by twice that angle.
So every angle of symmetry is a multiple of the smallest one.
note: Solution: the second angle is twice the first rotation.

question: True or False: (1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. (2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360.

parts.question: Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry.
If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360.

answer: Both are True.
steps: A full turn of 360° always brings any figure back to itself.
The smallest angle fits a whole number of times in 360°.
So a whole-number smallest angle is a factor of 360.
note: Statement 1 starts on the previous page of the book (bottom), statement 2 at the top of this one.

question: Is there a smallest angle of symmetry for all figures?
answer: No. Most figures have one, but a circle does not: every angle is an angle of symmetry for a circle.
steps: A figure like a square has smallest angle 90°.
A circle fits itself after any turn.
So there is no smallest angle for a circle.
note: Answer from the text.

question: Take a point on the rim of a circle and join it to the centre. Extend the segment to a diameter. Is that diameter a line of reflection symmetry?
answer: Yes. Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry.
steps: Fold the circle along a diameter.
The two halves overlap exactly.
This works for every diameter.
note: Answer from the text.

question: Like wheels, we can find other objects around us having rotational symmetry. Find them. (Shown: a three-bladed fan, a five-petal flower, a wheel with many spokes.)
answer: Open ended. Correct answers are objects that look the same after a turn less than 360°, for example a ceiling fan (3 angles), a flower with equal petals, a wheel with equal spokes, a windmill, the Ashoka Chakra.
steps: Look around for objects with equal parts around a centre.
Check by imagining a turn about the centre.
Name the object and the smallest angle of symmetry.
figure: Three pictures: a ceiling fan with 3 blades, a yellow flower with 5 petals, a wheel with 24 spokes.

book_label: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2, second block)
question: Colour the sectors of the circle below so that the figure has i) 3 angles of symmetry, ii) 4 angles of symmetry, iii) what are the possible numbers of angles of symmetry you can obtain by colouring the sectors in different ways? The circle is divided into 12 equal sectors.

parts.label: i
parts.question: 3 angles of symmetry

parts.label: ii
parts.question: 4 angles of symmetry

parts.label: iii
parts.question: Possible numbers of angles of symmetry

answer: i) Colour every 4th sector (3 coloured sectors, 120° apart). ii) Colour every 3rd sector (4 coloured sectors, 90° apart). iii) The number of angles of symmetry can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 (at most 12).
steps: Each sector is 360° ÷ 12 = 30°.
3 angles of symmetry need a pattern that repeats every 120°, that is every 4 sectors; 4 angles need a pattern repeating every 90°, every 3 sectors.
The pattern can repeat every 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 sectors, giving 12, 6, 4, 3, 2 or 1 angles of symmetry.
figure: Circle divided into 12 equal sectors by 6 diameters (each sector 30°).
note: Book solution says only '12 angles of symmetry are possible to obtain', and its pictures for (i) and (ii) show 3 and 3 adjacent coloured sectors, which would not give 3 and 4 angles. Answer here is computed (divisors of 12).

book_label: Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2, second block)
question: Draw two figures other than a circle and a square that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.
answer: Open ended. Examples: a plus sign of 4 equal arms (4 lines of symmetry, order 4), a four-petal flower (4 lines, order 4), an equilateral triangle (3 lines, order 3), a rectangle (2 lines, order 2).
steps: Choose a shape with equal parts around a centre.
Check that it can be folded to match itself.
Check that a turn less than 360° also fits.
figure: Solution shows a plus sign of two equal rectangles and a four-petal flower, each with 4 dashed lines of symmetry.

book_label: Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2, second block)
question: Draw, wherever possible, a rough sketch of: a. A triangle with at least two lines of symmetry and at least two angles of symmetry. b. A triangle with only one line of symmetry but not having rotational symmetry. c. A quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry. d. A quadrilateral with reflection symmetry but not having rotational symmetry.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Triangle with at least two lines and two angles of symmetry

parts.label: b
parts.question: Triangle with only one line of symmetry, no rotational symmetry

parts.label: c
parts.question: Quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry

parts.label: d
parts.question: Quadrilateral with reflection symmetry, no rotational symmetry

answer: a) Equilateral triangle: 3 lines, 3 angles (120°, 240°, 360°). b) Isosceles triangle (not equilateral): 1 line, no rotational symmetry. c) Parallelogram that is not a rectangle or rhombus: no line, angles 180° and 360°. d) Isosceles trapezium: 1 line, no rotational symmetry.
steps: (a) Only an equilateral triangle has 2 or more lines.
(b) An isosceles triangle folds one way only and fits only after 360°.
(c) A slanted parallelogram fits after a half turn but cannot be folded. (d) An isosceles trapezium folds down the middle but a half turn does not fit.
figure: Solution sketches: equilateral triangle with 3 dashed lines; isosceles triangle with 1 dashed line; slanted parallelogram; trapezium with equal slanting sides and 1 dashed line.
note: A 'Try This' marker appears beside this question in the book. Sketch tasks; all four are possible.

book_label: Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.2, second block)
question: In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry of this figure?
steps: Other angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle.

book_label: Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.2, second block)
question: In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry. The figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
steps: Angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle.
Two angles less than 60° means the smallest angle d and 2d are below 60°, and 3d = 60°.
note: Check: 20°, 40°, 60°: exactly two angles below 60°.

book_label: Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.2, second block)
question: Can we have a figure with rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: a. 45°? b. 17°?

parts.label: a
parts.question: Smallest angle of symmetry 45°

parts.label: b
parts.question: Smallest angle of symmetry 17°
parts.answer: No, since 360° is not a multiple of 17°

answer: a) Yes. b) No.
steps: The smallest angle must fit a whole number of times into 360°.
(a) 360 ÷ 45 = 8, so yes: 8 equal arms.
(b) 360 ÷ 17 is not a whole number (17 is not a factor of 360), so no.

book_label: Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.2, second block)
question: This is a picture of the new Parliament Building in Delhi; its outer boundary is a triangle-like shape with its three corners cut off (3 long sides alternating with 3 short sides). a. Does the outer boundary of the picture have reflection symmetry? If so, draw the lines of symmetries. How many are they? b. Does it have rotational symmetry around its centre? If so, find the angles of rotational symmetry.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Reflection symmetry? Number of lines

parts.label: b
parts.question: Rotational symmetry? Angles

answer: a) Yes, 3 lines of symmetry. b) Yes, 120°, 240°, 360°.
steps: The outline is a hexagon with 3 long sides and 3 short sides alternating.
Each line through the middle of a long side and the middle of the opposite short side is a line of symmetry: 3 lines.
It fits after a third of a turn: 360° ÷ 3 = 120°, so 120°, 240°, 360°.
figure: Photo of the Parliament Building and, beside it, its outline: a downward-pointing triangle with the three corners cut off.

book_label: Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.2, second block)
question: How many lines of symmetry do the shapes in the first shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Regular Polygons, have? What number sequence do you get? (The shapes are the regular triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon and decagon.)
answer: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10: the counting numbers starting from 3.
steps: A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry.
Triangle 3, quadrilateral 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6, heptagon 7, octagon 8, nonagon 9, decagon 10.
The sequence is the counting numbers from 3.
figure: Chapter 1 Table 3 first shape sequence: regular polygons from triangle (3 sides) to decagon (10 sides).
note: Chapter 1 table is not on these pages; shape list taken from the solution table.

book_label: Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.2, second block)
question: How many angles of symmetry do the shapes in the first shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Regular Polygons, have? What number sequence do you get? (Regular triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon, decagon.)
answer: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10: the counting numbers starting from 3.
steps: A regular polygon with n sides fits itself after each turn of 360° ÷ n.
So it has n angles of symmetry, counting 360°.
Triangle 3, square 4, ... decagon 10: the counting numbers from 3.
figure: Same regular polygon sequence from triangle to decagon.
note: No solution printed for Q9 in the solutions pages (the answer key jumps from Q8 to Q10); computed, same as Q8.

book_label: Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.2, second block)
question: How many lines of symmetry do the shapes in the last shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Koch Snowflake sequence, have? How many angles of symmetry?

parts.label: lines
parts.question: Lines of symmetry for the 5 shapes

parts.label: angles
parts.question: Angles of symmetry for the 5 shapes

answer: Lines of symmetry: 3, 6, 6, 6, 6. Angles of symmetry: 3, 6, 6, 6, 6.
steps: The first shape is a triangle: 3 lines and 3 angles.
From the next shape on, the snowflake has 6 lines and 6 angles.
The later shapes keep the same symmetry: 6 and 6.
figure: Chapter 1 Table 3 last shape sequence: Koch snowflake stages, from a triangle to snowflakes with finer points.
note: Figures are in Chapter 1; answer from the solutions.

book_label: Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.2, second block)
question: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does Ashoka Chakra have? (The Ashoka Chakra is a wheel with 24 equal spokes.)
answer: 24 lines of symmetry and 24 angles of symmetry.
steps: The Chakra has 24 equal spokes around the centre.
Each angle between spokes is 360° ÷ 24 = 15°.
Angles: 15°, 30°, ... 360°, which is 24 angles; also 24 lines.
figure: Blue Ashoka Chakra: a circle with 24 spokes.

question: Use the colour tiles given at the end of the book to complete the following figure so that it has exactly 2 lines of symmetry. (An 8 by 8 grid of square tiles, each divided by a diagonal into a blue and a yellow triangle. The top left 4 by 4 quarter is already filled. A red vertical line and a red horizontal line pass through the middle of the grid.)
answer: Fill the other three quarters as mirror images of the filled quarter in the red lines (reflect across the vertical line, then across the horizontal line). The result has exactly 2 lines of symmetry, the two red lines.
steps: Reflect the filled top-left quarter across the vertical red line into the top-right quarter.
Reflect the top half across the horizontal red line into the bottom half.
Check that no other fold line works.
figure: 8 by 8 grid of tiles, each square split diagonally into blue and yellow triangles; only the top-left 4 by 4 block is filled; red vertical and horizontal lines through the centre.
note: The grid is on its own page. 'Exactly 2 lines' assumes the filled quarter has no diagonal symmetry (its top-left tiles all slant the same way).

question: Use 16 such colour tiles to make figures that have exactly: 1 line of symmetry; 2 lines of symmetry.

parts.question: Figure with exactly 1 line of symmetry
parts.answer: 4 by 4 arrangement that matches itself in only one fold line

parts.question: Figure with exactly 2 lines of symmetry
parts.answer: 4 by 4 arrangement matching itself in two fold lines

answer: Open ended. A correct 4 by 4 arrangement has exactly one fold line (for example a vertical line) in the first case, and exactly two fold lines (for example vertical and horizontal) in the second.
steps: Lay 16 tiles in a 4 by 4 square.
For 1 line, make the left half a mirror image of the right half only.
For 2 lines, make it a mirror image both left to right and top to bottom, but not along the diagonals.

question: Use these colour tiles in making creative symmetric designs.
answer: Open ended. A correct design has at least one line of symmetry or rotational symmetry.
steps: Pick a few tiles and arrange them around a centre.
Repeat or mirror them so the design matches itself.
Check by folding or turning.

question: Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses. With what strategy can one play to win this game?
answer: The second player wins: after each move of the first player, place a line that is the 180° rotation about the centre of the grid of that move.
steps: The centre of the 6 by 6 grid is a corner point where 4 squares meet, so no line can cover it.
Every first-player move has a rotated copy that is free and does not overlap it.
So the second player always has a reply and the first player runs out of moves first.
figure: 6 by 6 grid with a few two-square lines drawn; a small picture marked 'Not allowed' showing two overlapping lines.
note: No strategy printed in the solutions; computed. A reflection across a middle line would fail because a line can lie across it, but the half turn always works.
